newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo to seek 20 pct reduction of its foreign debt.
newsitem.headline: Yugo to seek 20 pct reduction of its foreign debt.

text.p: Yugoslavia hopes to negotiate a 20 percent reduction in its total external debt, said a government report on the country's return to the world economy.

"Debt reorganisation is unavoidable. Reorganising will mean rescheduling, refinancing but above all a sizable debt and debt service reduction," said the Possible Policy Framework Paper, obtained by Reuters on Wednesday.
The report said accurate estimates for the country's debt are difficult to come by while negotiations continue on dividing the former Yugoslavia's assets and debts among its successor republics.
The Yugoslav government declines to release any official figures for the debt.

Dejan Jovovic of the Yugoslav trade ministry said in a study published earlier this year the most acceptable figure for Serbian and Montenegran gross external debt was around $9 billion, with principal and accumulated but unpaid interest.
"Yugoslavia aims to consolidate and reorganise the major part of its external debt," said the report, sent to the World Bank, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and commercial bank creditors.
Oskar Kovac, head of the country's team for negotiations with international credit institutions, said in an interview this was only what Yugoslavia proposed to its creditors.
He said contacts with the IMF and the World Bank meant Yugoslavia had begun to consolidate its external debt.
"Debt servicing would follow only after we agreed upon our debt reorganisation," he said.
It would be unrealistic to expect any substantial debt servicing before 2001, he added.
"Until that year Yugoslavia is expected to have trade and balance of payment deficits and will have to borrow to cover those gaps and increase its currency reserves," Kovac said.

Yugoslavia plans to start paying back interest on its debt in 1997. But any payment on principal would have to wait until 2001, when the government's economic forecasts say the country would have trade and balance of payment surpluses, Kovac said.
"We want to make things easier both for us and for our creditors, and pay interest. We did not want either side to live in a vacuum until the deal is completed.
"In the meantime, we would negotiate how to deal with the principal," he added.
If debt servicing had begun in 1996, it would have amounted to 141 percent of expected exports of goods and services.
It would take 43 percent of exports of goods and services, or 11 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP), just to handle the payments of interest, the report said.
Around 48 percent is owed to the Paris club creditors, about 20 percent to the World Bank and the IMF, and some 14 percent to the London club.
The report said all arrears and debt service obligations should be consolidated by the end of June 1997 and subjected to a multi-year rescheduling agreement.
"All obligations to repay principal should be reprogrammed (refinanced) from July 1997 onwards with a maturity of 20-1/2 years including a 5-1/2 year grace period," the report said.
Half of the accrued interest on the Paris club debt and 25 percent of interest on the London club debt would be capitalised and rescheduled under the above terms.
All reorganised debt should carry the interest rate of no more than six percent, said the report.
Those estimates assume a gradual increase in direct foreign investment to some $460 million a year in 2005.
"We have also taken into account cumulative debt-to-equity swaps of some $350 million over the next four years," Kovac said.

All projections assumed the economy would grow an average of 7.1 percent a year through 2005. By 2001, Yugoslavia's GDP is estimated to reach $26.6 to $27 billion from the $15.5 billion expected for 1996. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
